newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: COFFEE--Colombian growers declare debtors' strike.
newsitem.headline: COFFEE--Colombian growers declare debtors' strike.

text.p: Colombia's leading independent coffee growers' association declared a moratorium on debt payments on Wednesday as part of a campaign of "civil disobedience" aimed at helping cash-strapped farmers.

The decision, which would affect about $200 million in past-due loans owed to the state-run Caja Agraria bank and Banco Cafetero -- partly owned by the government-affiliated National Coffee Growers' Federation -- was adopted at a meeting of the independent Unidad Cafetera Nacional in the western city of Pereira.

The UCN, a loosely-woven organisation which maintains a strong presence in most of Colombia's coffee-growing region, has long criticised the federation and policies that it says have crippled the coffee sector.

Jorge Enrique Robledo, its national coordinator, told Reuters in a telephone interview from Pereira that 650 delegates participated in Wednesday's meeting and unanimously approved what amounts to a debtors' strike.

The delegates represented growers in 102 municipalities scattered across nine different Colombian provinces, he added, saying there was a clear consensus about the need for deep-rooted reform of Colombia's coffee industry.
To give an idea of the extent of the debt moratorium, and its potential impact on the economy, Robledo said 50,000 coffee growers currently face legal problems because of past-due loans.
In Caldas alone, one of the country's main coffee-producing provinces, 32 percent of the Caja Agraria's loan portfolio consists of past-due obligations.

Asked how independent growers would respond if banks foreclosed on their loans and moved to seize their assets and property, Robledo defiantly said "civil disobedience" could escalate into "civil resistance."
"We're not going to let anyone's land be taken away from them," he said.
Growers attending the meeting also agreed to press for a sharp increase in Colombia's internal coffee price and for government assistance in restructuring their debts.
Colombia's internal coffee price was raised by 12 percent to 248,125 pesos per 125-kg load last week in a bid to bring it closer into line with recent increases in world market prices.
But Robledo said this had failed to quell widespread discontent among growers, and that the UCN would now push for a price hike up to 290,000 pesos per load.
"The price should be stable and guaranteed by the government," Robledo said, adding that there was no reason growers should remain "at the mercy of speculation."

Coffee farmers have long complained of growing levels of indebtedness and impoverishment, and a lack of government aid to stop it. The situation, and quiet desperation of some growers, goes a long way toward explaining why police say opium poppies have been cropping lately on coffee plantations in Caldas and Risaralda province, of which Pereira is the capital.

Robledo said participants in Wednesday's meeting had also agreed to press the government for access to new sources of credit, since most growers were "on the blacklists of banks" and no longer had any place to borrow money.
Government spokesmen and officials with the National Coffee Growers' Federation could not be reached for immediate comment.
